1. Prima che + subjunctive / prima di + infinitive
As in chapter 34: with the SAME subject use "prima di + infinitive"; with a DIFFERENT subject, "prima che + subjunctive":
Lo controllo prima che arrivi il parroco.
"Prima che" ALWAYS takes the subjunctive: "prima che arrivi", NOT "prima che arriva". In the past: "prima che arrivasse".
"Finché" (until) takes the INDICATIVE. The "non" that follows is purely stylistic:
Stay at home until you feel better.
Without "non", "finché" can also mean "as long as": "Finché sei qui, sono felice" (As long as you're here, I'm happy).
Unlike "prima che", "dopo che" takes the INDICATIVE (a real fact, already happened). A compound tense is often used:
I'll finish the varnish after you've finished the retouching.
After the priest had left, we celebrated.
After you've finished, you can rest.
NOT "dopo che sia partito". Correct: "dopo che è partito". It's a common mistake even among Italians, who mix it up with "prima che".
4. Non appena, da quando, ogni volta che, nel momento in cui
Non appena è asciutta, la ritocchi.
Da quando lavora qui, è felice.
Ogni volta che starnutisce, beve un tè.
Nel momento in cui lo vede, piange.
All of these take the INDICATIVE. For the future, Italian prefers the future tense: "Non appena arriverà, ti chiamo."
5. Man mano che: as, gradually as
As we finish, I'll send you the photos.
As she cleaned, the colours reappeared.
As she grows, Viola talks more and more.
As soon as it's dry, you retouch it.
Every time she sneezes, she drinks a cup of tea.

Since arriving at the workshop, Chiara had worked on the Prato Annunciation every day, from nine to six, with the patience of someone who knows a painting can't be hurried. Before touching anything, she had photographed it, measured it and studied it under the microscope. Then she had begun to clean, one centimetre at a time, and as the yellowed varnish disappeared, the sixteenth-century colours came back to light: the blue of the Virgin's cloak, the pink of her cheeks, the gold of the rays.

The problem was the angel. Or rather, its left wing, where a piece of paint the size of a coin was missing. Chiara had decided from the start that she would retouch it last, after everything else had been finished. "It's like dessert at the end of dinner," she said. "Before dessert comes, you have to eat everything else." Bellini, on Saturdays, watched her work in silence and nodded.

To prepare, Chiara had asked Davide for help. Every Saturday, after the visitors had gone, the boy sat in front of the angel and drew the undamaged right wing, feather by feather. As the drawings piled up, Chiara studied them like a map: which way the light came from, how long the brushstrokes were, where the painter had hesitated. "When I retouch the left one," she said, "it'll be as if he had drawn it himself."

Then, on the first of December, disaster struck. While Matei was moving the painting to photograph it, he noticed that a small crack in the wood, which until then had been stable, had widened overnight. It had to be consolidated before anything else could be done, and the glue needed two days to dry. The calendar had suddenly shrunk like a badly washed jumper.

On the second of December Chiara woke up with a temperature. Thirty-eight and a half. She came to the workshop anyway, with her scarf up to her nose and a thermos of camomile, and Giulia sent her home with a formal order: "Don't come back until your temperature is normal. Signed: the management." Chiara went home. But every time she woke up in bed, she sent a message: "The crack? The glue? The angel?"

Meanwhile Matei and Giulia worked in the evenings too. Viola slept in her playpen under the window, wrapped in Doina's white blanket, and every time she woke up she said "guadda" and went back to sleep. Graziella came up to protest at ten, at eleven and at midnight. "Until you go to bed, I won't sleep," she threatened. Then, before going back down, she left a plate of biscuits and a thermos of coffee on the table.

On the fourth of December, with her temperature still at thirty-eight, she came back. She sat down in front of the easel and said, before anyone could protest: "The angel's wing is mine. I've waited three months for it. I'm not leaving it to anyone else." Giulia looked at Matei. Matei looked at Giulia. Bellini, who had dropped by "by chance" even though it was Wednesday, said only: "Let her work. My grandfather restored with a temperature of forty."

They decided to work all together, in shifts, until the painting was finished. Matei consolidated the crack and checked the glue every two hours. Giulia prepared the final varnish. Chiara, wrapped in a blanket, retouched the wing one millimetre at a time, with the smallest brush in the workshop. Every time she sneezed, she had to stop, step away from the painting and drink a cup of tea: management's orders. She sneezed a lot.

The others did their part too. Graziella brought hot soup every three hours, because, she said, "no angel was ever restored on an empty stomach". Pietro, after finishing his homework, took Lupino out in front of the workshop, so that nobody had to stop working. Davide, in the afternoons, sat next to Chiara and passed her the brushes without a word, like an assistant in an operating theatre.

On the night of the fifth of December, at three o'clock, Chiara put down her brush. In the workshop there was only her and Matei, who was asleep on a chair with his head against the wall. The wing was finished. You could no longer see where the sixteenth-century paint ended and Chiara's began. She stood looking at it for a long time, without moving, until the light of the lamp began to flicker. Then she woke Matei. "Look," she told him. It was the only word that came to mind.

Matei looked. Then he looked at Chiara. Her eyes were red from fever and tiredness, and she had a smile he had never seen on her before. "In all the time I've been doing this job," he said softly, "I've seen few retouches like this. Bellini would be proud." Chiara began to laugh and cry at the same time, then sneezed three times, and Matei sent her home in a taxi before she could object.

On the morning of the sixth, Giulia applied the final varnish. Then they all waited, watching the clock, until the varnish was dry. By the evening of the seventh the painting was ready, packed in a wooden crate, with a label handwritten by Chiara: "Annunciation, church of San Domenico, Prato. Fragile. With love."

On the evening of the seventh, before the crate was closed, Bellini arrived with a small ultraviolet lamp in his pocket. "Before it leaves, I want to see it," he said. He switched off the lights and passed the lamp over the wing, slowly, centimetre by centimetre. Under ultraviolet light, recent retouches usually show up at once. This time Bellini had to search for a long time. In the end he switched the light back on and said nothing. But he left whistling.

On the eighth of December, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, the church of San Domenico was full. The parish priest, an elderly, sturdy man with a baritone voice, had had the painting placed on an easel by the altar, covered with a white cloth. The moment he removed the cloth, an absolute silence fell over the church. Then a lady in the front row said, far too loudly: "Holy Mother, the angel is flying!"

Chiara was in the third row, with her scarf round her neck and a handkerchief in her hand, still a little feverish. The priest looked for her and, before she could hide, called her up to the altar in front of everyone. "This is the young lady who gave our angel back its wings," he said into the microphone. "With a temperature, I'm told. From today, every time someone looks at this painting, they'll say a little prayer for her too."

On the way back, on the train to Florence, Chiara fell asleep after five minutes, her head on Giulia's shoulder. Giulia took out her phone and wrote a message to Bellini, who hadn't been able to come: "Mission accomplished. The angel is flying. Chiara has finished her probation." The reply came a minute later, in a single word, as always: "Hired."

That evening, at home, Chiara phoned her mother in Bologna. She told her everything: the crack, the fever, the nights, the angel, the lady who had shouted in church. Her mother listened in silence to the end. Then she said: "Grandma always used to say it. Before you touch a fabric, look at it until it speaks to you. You looked at that angel until it started to fly." Chiara didn't answer. She had already fallen asleep, phone in hand.
